definition: In the history of artificial intelligence (AI), an AI winter is a period of reduced funding and interest in AI research.
details: The field has experienced several hype cycles, followed by disappointment and criticism, followed by funding cuts, followed by renewed interest years or even decades later. The term first appeared in 1984 as the topic of a public debate at the annual meeting of AAAI (then called the "American Association of Artificial Intelligence"). Roger Schank and Marvin Minsky—two leading AI researchers who experienced the "winter" of the 1970s—warned the business community that enthusiasm for AI had spiraled out of control in the 1980s and that disappointment would certainly follow. They described a chain reaction, similar to a "nuclear winter", that would begin with pessimism in the AI community, followed by pessimism in the press, followed by a severe cutback in funding, followed by the end of serious research. Three years later the billion-dollar AI industry began to collapse. There were two major "winters", which lasted approximately from 1974–1980 and 1987–2000, and several smaller episodes, including the following: 1966: failure of machine translation 1969: criticism of perceptrons (early, single-layer artificial neural networks) 1971–75: DARPA's frustration with the Speech Understanding

explainer.lead: An AI winter is a period when excitement about artificial intelligence gives way to disappointment, reduced funding, and less research activity. It matters because technical promises can shape budgets, careers, and entire research programmes long before their limitations become clear.

tiers.eli5: Imagine planting a garden because everyone promises amazing flowers, then stopping when the flowers do not appear as quickly as expected. An AI winter is like that: people become disappointed with AI, money and attention dry up, and fewer researchers can continue their work. Interest can return years later when new ideas or results restore confidence.
tiers.practitioner: For engineers, AI winter is a useful lens for assessing the gap between demonstrated capability and expectations around a project. A disappointing result does not necessarily make an approach worthless: perceptron research lost mainstream support even though important theoretical neural-network work continued. The practical pitfall is treating either excitement or pessimism as evidence of technical performance rather than testing systems on real problems.
tiers.paperLevel: An AI winter is formally a historical period of reduced funding and interest in AI research, often following a cycle of inflated expectations, disappointment, criticism, and funding cuts. The term appeared at a 1984 AAAI panel discussion, where researchers warned of a chain reaction from community pessimism to press pessimism, severe funding reductions, and the end of serious research. The two major winters are dated approximately 1974–1980 and 1987–2000; these are broad historical periods, not precise measurements of research activity.

explainer.example: Early machine translation attracted strong US government support during the Cold War, but researchers underestimated problems such as word-sense disambiguation. In 1966, ALPAC concluded that machine translation was more expensive, less accurate, and slower than human translation; after roughly 20 million dollars had been spent, the NRC ended its support.

usedIn.name: Machine translation
usedIn.detail: The 1966 ALPAC report found machine translation slower, less accurate, and more expensive than human translation, after which NRC support ended.

usedIn.name: Neural-network research
usedIn.detail: Criticism of perceptrons in 1969 contributed to a long period in which major funding for neural-network approaches was difficult to find.

usedIn.name: UK academic AI
usedIn.detail: The 1973 Lighthill report led to a large contraction, with research continuing at only a few universities.

usedIn.name: Expert systems
usedIn.detail: Many expert systems were abandoned during the 1990s, one of the episodes associated with the second major winter.

explainer.intuition: AI research depends on confidence as well as technical progress. When ambitious promises repeatedly fail, that confidence can collapse, making even worthwhile research harder to fund until new results revive interest.
howItWorks: Optimism and impressive demonstrations create high expectations.
Funding and investment expand around the promised capabilities.
Technical limits or disappointing real-world results become visible.
Criticism spreads through the research community and press.
Budgets are cut, projects end, and research interest contracts until a later revival.
explainer.whyItMatters: AI winters show how expectations and funding decisions can accelerate or interrupt scientific progress. Remembering them helps researchers, funders, and businesses judge demonstrations carefully and distinguish temporary disappointment from the long-term value of a research direction.
misconceptions: An AI winter does not mean all AI research stops; important work can continue with little funding.
A single failed project is not an AI winter; the term describes a broader decline in funding and interest.
A winter is not proof that the underlying goals are impossible, since later advances can revive the field.
